Reminder: Installing vs. Loading Packages

Packages are add-ons that give R extra functions (e.g., psych, ggplot2). Using one is a two-step process:


Step 1: install.packages("name")
Downloads the package onto your computer

○ Only need to do this once per computer


○ Package name goes in quotes


○ Needs an internet connection


install.packages("psych")


Step 2: library(name)
Loads the package into your current R session so its functions are available

○ Need to do this every time you open R / RStudio


○ Quotes are optional


○ Put it at the top of your script


library(psych)



Installing is like buying a book; library() is taking it off the shelf to read it. Installing alone is not enough: without library(), you’ll see could not find function "describeBy".

title: Measures of Variability
text:
Descriptives by Group
Aggregation involves summarizing or grouping data based on certain variables.
Commonly used to calculate summary statistics like mean, variance, or sum for each group.


Benefits:

○ Data summary


○ Data simplification


○ Statistical analysis


○ Trend identification


○ Data privacy


○ Data-driven decisions


aggregate(y ~ group, FUN)

○ y = vector we want statistics for


○ group = vector with grouping data


○ FUN = function to apply

section: Descriptives by Group: table() and describeBy()
text:
Descriptives by Group: table() and describeBy()


Crosstab (counts): table(var1, var2)

○ var1 = rows, var2 = columns (both categorical)


iris$Size <- cut(iris$Sepal.Length,
                 breaks = c(0, 5.8, 10),
                 labels = c("Short", "Long"))

table(iris$Species, iris$Size)

            
             Short Long
  setosa        50    0
  versicolor    24   26
  virginica      6   44



All descriptives at once: describeBy(x, group)

○ From the psych package: install.packages("psych")


○ x = numeric vector, group = grouping vector


○ Add mat = TRUE for one compact table


library(psych)

describeBy(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Species,
           mat = TRUE)[, c("group1", "n", "mean",
                           "sd", "median")]

        group1  n  mean        sd median
X11     setosa 50 5.006 0.3524897    5.0
X12 versicolor 50 5.936 0.5161711    5.9
X13  virginica 50 6.588 0.6358796    6.5

title: Measures of Variability
text:
Visualizations: Boxplots


Back to the iris dataset, distribution of Sepal Length by species
Anatomy of a boxplot:

○ “Minimum”


○ 25th Quantile (Q1)


○ Median


○ 75th Quantile (Q3)


○ “Maximum”


○ Points representing outliers











“Minimum” and “maximum” are not the true min and max

○ Minimum: \(Q1 - 1.5 * IQR\)


○ Maximum: \(Q3 + 1.5 * IQR\)

Means that the whiskers contain ~99% of the data, rest are outliers


For more explanation of the anatomy of a boxplot, feel free to check this post out from Statistics by Jim

section: Where Does R Look for Files? The Working Directory
text:
Where Does R Look for Files? The Working Directory

When you write read.csv("student_data.csv"), R reads it as: “look for student_data.csv inside the current working directory”


Rule for beginners

Your R Markdown file and all required data files should be placed in the same assignment folder before you begin working.

Lab_03/
├── Lab_03.Rmd
└── student_data.csv
Then loading the data only needs the file name:

student_data <- read.csv("student_data.csv")


Check before you load data

getwd()        # which folder is R looking in?
list.files()   # which files can R see there?

If the setup is correct you should see something like:
[1] "/Users/yourname/Documents/Lab_03"
[1] "Lab_03.Rmd"  "student_data.csv"

○ Tip: when you knit an .Rmd, the working directory is the folder the .Rmd is saved in

title: Measures of Variability
text:
The Common Mistake



Files downloaded to different places
Downloads/
└── Lab_03.Rmd

Desktop/
└── student_data.csv
The working directory is Downloads, so this fails:

read.csv("student_data.csv")

Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
  cannot open file 'student_data.csv': No such file or directory

What the error means
R looked in the working directory but did not find a file with that exact name.
The fix

○ Move both files into the same folder (e.g., Lab_03/)


○ Open the .Rmd from that folder


○ Re-run getwd() and list.files() to confirm


Fix the folder, not the code: don’t keep rewriting the path in read.csv().
Also check the exact file name: Student_Data.csv ≠ student_data.csv

R Functions
We’ve seen some built-in R functions (e.g., mean(), median()), but we can also make our own


function_name <- function(argument) {
  do some stuff
  return(this stuff)
}

ⓘ Don’t actually need to call return(); R will automatically return the last expression


Then, you can call the function

To keep the results, make sure to assign them to some variable

title: Central Tendency
text:
Measures of Variability in R
Variance: Average of the squared distances of each value from the mean \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\)
Standard deviation: Square root of the variance; the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the original units
Quantile: A cut point that splits sorted data into equal-sized groups (e.g., 25% of values fall below the 1st quartile, 75% below the 3rd)
IQR: 3rd quartile minus 1st quartile; the range of the middle 50% of the data

Let’s Do Some Visualization
Base R Graphics: Bar Chart


Useful to show frequency/percentage of categorical data

○ Categorical data: not numerically meaningful, it’s a category of a type

X-axis displays the variable; Y-axis displays frequency
Bars do not touch and have equal widths
Should not be 3-dimensional!
barplot() function

○ height = a table of counts (use table() first!)


○ main, xlab, ylab, col work the same as hist()

title: Central Tendency
text:
Histogram vs. Bar Chart


Histogram

○ Interval/ratio (numeric) data


○ Bars touch: continuity of the data


○ hist(x)


Bar chart

○ Categorical data


○ Bars do not touch: separate categories


○ barplot(table(x))


Try it: make a bar chart of mtcars$cyl (number of cylinders)

title: Central Tendency
text:
Let’s Do Some Visualization
Base R Graphics: Pie Chart


Categorical data only
Never use with more than 2–3 categories
Use bar charts for comparisons
If unsure, don’t use a pie chart!!

Why?

○ Eye is good at judging relative linear measures, not relative areas


○ Anything a pie chart can show, a bar chart can show better (Cleveland, 1985)


pie() function

○ x = a table of counts, just like barplot()
